# Py Lab 5 {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Visualisation and description {.smaller}

The lecture established that adult asthma prevalence barely varies across Pennsylvania
counties — 9.7% to 11.6% — while smoking prevalence varies across eleven points, and that the
two move together at **+0.659**.

This lab builds twelve figures from five real files, then repairs three figures that run
without error and mislead anyway.

::: {.callout-note}
## Lab mechanics
- Each exercise supplies a worked example, then a similar problem to complete.
- Click into a code block and press **Run**. Edit the blanks (`____`) and run again.
- **Hint** gives the reasoning. **Solution** gives the answer.
- Each exercise takes two slides: the worked example, then the task.
- Arrow keys navigate between slides.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Three of these exercises contain no error message
Exercises 9, 10, and 11 supply figures that execute cleanly and state something false. A
figure that raises no exception has not been checked — it has only been run.
:::

## The data {.smaller}

Five real files, all mounted and readable with `pd.read_csv()`.

| File | Rows | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv` | 67 | Asthma, **smoking**, obesity prevalence — CDC PLACES 2024 |
| `data/pa_counties.csv` | 67 | Population, **region**, **metro/nonmetro** — the join target |
| `data/pa_maternal_infant.csv` | 67 | Infant mortality, poverty, income — 23 counties suppressed |
| `data/pa_covid_monthly.csv` | 3,283 | COVID deaths by county and month, 2020–2024 |
| `data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv` | 402 | Overdose deaths and rates, 2019–2024 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Three facts that recur throughout
**A rate is** `deaths / population * 100000`. **A blank is suppression**, not zero. Neither
`region` nor `metro` appears in any outcome file, so every grouped figure below requires a
join first.
:::

## The course figure palette {.smaller}

Every colour below was measured against white with the WCAG relative luminance formula. A
mark that carries data needs **3:1**; text needs **4.5:1**.

| Colour | Ratio | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `#003594` royal | **10.84 : 1** | The primary series |
| `#8a6400` dark gold | **5.38 : 1** | The second series |
| `#6b7280` gray | **4.83 : 1** | Annotation and source notes |

::: {.callout-warning}
## No two of these separate from each other by 3:1
Royal against dark gold is **2.02:1**. Each is readable against the page; they are not
reliably distinguishable from one another. **Every two-series figure in this lab therefore
carries a second channel** — a marker shape, a dash pattern, or a direct label.
:::

# Exercise 1 — A figure is a figure and an axes {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 1 — A figure is a figure and an axes {.smaller}

**Worked example.** `plt.subplots()` returns two objects: the **figure** is the canvas, and the
**axes** is one set of coordinates drawn on it. Nearly every figure begins with this call.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of adult smoking prevalence across 67 Pennsylvania counties, spread from about 10.6 to 21.8 percent with most counties between 15 and 19 percent."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.hist(asthma["smoking_prev_pct"], bins=10, color="#003594", edgecolor="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")
ax.set_title("Smoking prevalence across 67 PA counties")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 1.** Histogram of adult smoking prevalence across 67 Pennsylvania counties, spread from about 10.6 to 21.8 percent with most counties between 15 and 19 percent.
:::

# Exercise 2 — Bars compare categories {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 2 — Bars compare categories {.smaller}

**Worked example.** `ax.bar()` compares one value across named categories. Sorting before
plotting delivers the ranking to the reader for free.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the five Pennsylvania counties with the highest adult smoking prevalence, ranging from about 20.7 to 21.8 percent."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
top5 = asthma.nlargest(5, "smoking_prev_pct").sort_values("smoking_prev_pct")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.barh(top5["county"], top5["smoking_prev_pct"], color="#003594")
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title("Five highest county smoking rates")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 2.** Horizontal bar chart of the five Pennsylvania counties with the highest adult smoking prevalence, ranging from about 20.7 to 21.8 percent.
:::

## Exercise 2 — Bars compare categories — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw the five counties with the **lowest** smoking prevalence. Use
`.nsmallest()`, and sort so the bars run in order.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
bottom5 = asthma.____(5, "smoking_prev_pct").sort_values("smoking_prev_pct")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.barh(bottom5["county"], bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"], color="#003594")
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title("Five lowest county smoking rates")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(bottom5[["county", "smoking_prev_pct"]].to_string(index=False))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars
#| hint: true
# The blank is nsmallest.
#
# .nlargest(n, col) and .nsmallest(n, col) both return whole rows, not
# just the column — which is why `bottom5["county"]` still works.
# Chester should come out at the bottom, at 10.6%.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
bottom5 = asthma.nsmallest(5, "smoking_prev_pct").sort_values("smoking_prev_pct")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.barh(bottom5["county"], bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"], color="#003594")
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title("Five lowest county smoking rates")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(bottom5[["county", "smoking_prev_pct"]].to_string(index=False))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars
#| check: true
assert len(bottom5) == 5, "Five counties."
assert bottom5["county"].iloc[0] == "Chester", "Chester has the lowest smoking prevalence, 10.6%."
assert abs(bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"].min() - 10.6) < 0.001, "The minimum is 10.6%."
assert bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"].is_monotonic_increasing, "Sort before plotting."
assert len(ax.patches) == 5, "Five bars must be drawn."
```

# Exercise 3 — A histogram shows a distribution {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 3 — A histogram shows a distribution {.smaller}

**Worked example.** A histogram bins a continuous variable and counts what lands in each bin.
`ax.axvline()` adds a reference line, identified in the title so colour is not the only cue.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of adult smoking prevalence across 67 counties with a dashed vertical line marking the state mean of 17.1 percent."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
state_mean = asthma["smoking_prev_pct"].mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.hist(asthma["smoking_prev_pct"], bins=12, color="#003594", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(state_mean, color="#8a6400", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")
ax.set_title(f"Smoking prevalence (dashed line = mean, {state_mean:.1f}%)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 3.** Histogram of adult smoking prevalence across 67 counties with a dashed vertical line marking the state mean of 17.1 percent.
:::

## Exercise 3 — A histogram shows a distribution — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw the distribution of **infant mortality** across the counties that publish a
rate, and mark the **median** with a dashed line.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex3_histogram
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])

state_median = reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"].____()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.hist(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"], bins=10, color="#003594", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(state_median, color="#8a6400", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality, 44 reporting counties (dashed = median, {state_median:.1f})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("counties plotted:", len(reporting))
print("median:", round(state_median, 2))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex3_histogram
#| hint: true
# The blank is median.
#
# .dropna(subset=[...]) removes only the rows missing that column, so 44
# counties survive — the 23 suppressed ones are gone. Say so in the title,
# as the code already does. A figure that silently drops a third of the
# state is the kind of figure this course is trying not to produce.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex3_histogram
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])

state_median = reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"].median()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.hist(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"], bins=10, color="#003594", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(state_median, color="#8a6400", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality, 44 reporting counties (dashed = median, {state_median:.1f})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("counties plotted:", len(reporting))
print("median:", round(state_median, 2))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex3_histogram
#| check: true
assert len(reporting) == 44, "44 counties publish an infant mortality rate."
assert abs(state_median - 6.0) < 0.001, "The median is 6.0 per 1,000."
assert len(ax.lines) >= 1, "Draw the median as a vertical line."
assert ax.get_xlabel() != "" and ax.get_ylabel() != "", "Label both axes."
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The 44 belongs in the title
Twenty-three counties are absent from this figure, and they are disproportionately rural.
A reader who is not told that will read it as a picture of Pennsylvania.
:::

# Exercise 4 — Scatter shows co-movement {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 4 — Scatter shows co-movement {.smaller}

**Worked example.** `ax.scatter()` places one point per row, using two columns as coordinates.
It is the figure to draw before trusting any correlation.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of adult asthma prevalence against adult smoking prevalence across 67 Pennsylvania counties, rising from left to right with a correlation of 0.659."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
r = asthma["smoking_prev_pct"].corr(asthma["asthma_prev_pct"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.scatter(asthma["smoking_prev_pct"], asthma["asthma_prev_pct"],
           color="#003594", s=40, alpha=0.8, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title(f"Asthma against smoking, 67 counties (r = {r:.3f})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 4.** Scatter plot of adult asthma prevalence against adult smoking prevalence across 67 Pennsylvania counties, rising from left to right with a correlation of 0.659.
:::

## Exercise 4 — Scatter shows co-movement — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw infant mortality against **child poverty** for the reporting counties, and
put the correlation in the title.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])

r = reporting["children_in_poverty_pct"].____(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.scatter(reporting["children_in_poverty_pct"], reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"],
           color="#003594", s=40, alpha=0.8, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Children in poverty (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality against child poverty, 44 counties (r = {r:.3f})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("r =", round(r, 3))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
#| hint: true
# The blank is corr.
#
# series_a.corr(series_b) returns a single number between -1 and +1.
# You should get +0.646 — a strong positive relationship for county-level
# public health data. Remember what it does not say: these are counties,
# not families, and the figure cannot establish a cause.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])

r = reporting["children_in_poverty_pct"].corr(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.scatter(reporting["children_in_poverty_pct"], reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"],
           color="#003594", s=40, alpha=0.8, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Children in poverty (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality against child poverty, 44 counties (r = {r:.3f})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("r =", round(r, 3))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
#| check: true
assert abs(r - 0.6465) < 0.01, "Child poverty and infant mortality correlate at +0.646."
assert len(ax.collections) >= 1, "ax.scatter must draw the points."
assert "0.6" in ax.get_title(), "Put the correlation in the title."
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## This is a statement about counties
Counties with more children in poverty bury more infants. The mechanism is structural —
prenatal care access, distance to obstetric services, housing, and food security. The figure
describes counties, never individual families.
:::

# Exercise 5 — A line needs an ordered axis {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 5 — A line needs an ordered axis {.smaller}

**Worked example.** A line asserts that consecutive points are connected. That claim is only
meaningful when the x-axis has an order, such as time. `pd.to_datetime()` supplies it.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of monthly COVID-19 deaths in Allegheny County from March 2020 through March 2024, with peaks in winter 2020 and winter 2021 and a decline to near zero afterwards."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])

allegheny = covid[covid["county"] == "Allegheny"].sort_values("month")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3))
ax.plot(allegheny["month"], allegheny["covid_deaths"], color="#003594", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("COVID-19 deaths")
ax.set_title("Monthly COVID-19 deaths, Allegheny County")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 5.** Line chart of monthly COVID-19 deaths in Allegheny County from March 2020 through March 2024, with peaks in winter 2020 and winter 2021 and a decline to near zero afterwards.
:::

## Exercise 5 — A line needs an ordered axis — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw the **statewide** monthly total. Group by month and sum across all counties.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_line
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])

statewide = covid.____("month")["covid_deaths"].sum()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3))
ax.plot(statewide.index, statewide.values, color="#003594", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("COVID-19 deaths")
ax.set_title("Statewide monthly COVID-19 deaths")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("months:", len(statewide))
print("peak:", statewide.idxmax().date(), "=", statewide.max())
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_line
#| hint: true
# The blank is groupby.
#
# Grouping by month and summing gives one number per month across all 67
# counties. The result is a Series whose index is the month, which is why
# the plot call uses .index and .values.
# The peak is January 2022 — Omicron — at 4,294 deaths.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_line
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])

statewide = covid.groupby("month")["covid_deaths"].sum()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3))
ax.plot(statewide.index, statewide.values, color="#003594", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("COVID-19 deaths")
ax.set_title("Statewide monthly COVID-19 deaths")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("months:", len(statewide))
print("peak:", statewide.idxmax().date(), "=", statewide.max())
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex5_line
#| check: true
assert len(statewide) == 49, "The file covers 49 months."
assert statewide.max() == 4294, "The peak month is 4,294 deaths."
assert str(statewide.idxmax().date()) == "2022-01-01", "The peak is January 2022."
assert len(ax.lines) >= 1, "ax.plot must draw the line."
```

# Exercise 6 — Two series need two channels {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 6 — Two series need two channels {.smaller}

**Worked example.** Royal and dark gold each pass contrast against the page, but separate from
each other by only 2.02:1. A second channel — here a marker shape plus a legend — is what makes
the groups distinguishable.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of adult obesity against adult smoking prevalence for 67 Pennsylvania counties, with metro counties drawn as circles and nonmetro counties as triangles, plus a legend."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "metro"]], on="county", how="left")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
for group, colour, marker in [("Metro", "#003594", "o"), ("Nonmetro", "#8a6400", "^")]:
    subset = joined[joined["metro"] == group]
    ax.scatter(subset["smoking_prev_pct"], subset["obesity_prev_pct"],
               color=colour, marker=marker, s=42, label=group)
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Adult obesity prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title("Obesity against smoking, by metro status")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 6.** Scatter plot of adult obesity against adult smoking prevalence for 67 Pennsylvania counties, with metro counties drawn as circles and nonmetro counties as triangles, plus a legend.
:::

## Exercise 6 — Two series need two channels — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw **asthma** against smoking with the same two-channel treatment. Add the
legend that makes the markers readable.

# Exercise 7 — Multi-panel figures {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 7 — Multi-panel figures {.smaller}

**Worked example.** `plt.subplots(rows, cols)` returns a 2-D array of axes, indexed
`axes[row, col]` — the NumPy indexing from Module 3. Building the panels in a loop prevents the
copy-paste errors that hand-written panels breed.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side histograms of Pennsylvania county distributions: adult smoking prevalence on the left and adult obesity prevalence on the right."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3))

panels = [
    (axes[0], asthma["smoking_prev_pct"], "Adult smoking (%)"),
    (axes[1], asthma["obesity_prev_pct"], "Adult obesity (%)"),
]

for panel, values, label in panels:
    panel.hist(values, bins=10, color="#003594", edgecolor="white")
    panel.set_title(label, fontsize=9)
    panel.set_ylabel("Counties", fontsize=8)

fig.suptitle("Two county-level distributions", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 7.** Two side-by-side histograms of Pennsylvania county distributions: adult smoking prevalence on the left and adult obesity prevalence on the right.
:::

## Exercise 7 — Multi-panel figures — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Build a **2 × 2** grid of the four distributions listed below. Index the bottom
row correctly.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_subplots
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 4.4))

panels = [
    (axes[0, 0], asthma["asthma_prev_pct"],           "Adult asthma (%)"),
    (axes[0, 1], asthma["smoking_prev_pct"],          "Adult smoking (%)"),
    (axes[____, 0], births["infant_mortality_per_1000"], "Infant deaths per 1,000"),
    (axes[1, 1], births["children_in_poverty_pct"],   "Children in poverty (%)"),
]

for panel, values, label in panels:
    panel.hist(values.dropna(), bins=10, color="#003594", edgecolor="white")
    panel.set_title(label, fontsize=9)
    panel.tick_params(labelsize=7)

fig.suptitle("Four county-level distributions, Pennsylvania", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("grid shape:", axes.shape)
print("panels drawn:", sum(1 for a in axes.flat if len(a.patches) > 0))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_subplots
#| hint: true
# The blank is 1.
#
# axes is a 2-D NumPy array. Row 0 is the top, row 1 is the bottom, and
# the column index comes second — axes[1, 0] is bottom-left.
# .flat walks every panel regardless of shape, which is how the count
# at the end works.
```

# Exercise 8 — Rates against counts {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 8 — Rates against counts {.smaller}

**Worked example.** A count of events largely measures how many people live somewhere. Ranking
counties by total COVID deaths returns the five largest counties.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")

totals = (covid.groupby("county", as_index=False)["covid_deaths"].sum()
               .merge(counties[["county", "population_2023"]], on="county"))

print(totals.nlargest(5, "covid_deaths")[["county", "covid_deaths", "population_2023"]]
            .to_string(index=False))
print()
print("deaths vs population:", round(totals["covid_deaths"].corr(totals["population_2023"]), 3))
```

## Exercise 8 — Rates against counts — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Compute deaths per 100,000 and rank by the **rate**. Compare the two lists.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_rates
import pandas as pd

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")

totals = (covid.groupby("county", as_index=False)["covid_deaths"].sum()
               .merge(counties[["county", "population_2023"]], on="county"))

totals["rate_per_100k"] = totals["covid_deaths"] / totals["____"] * 100000

by_count = totals.nlargest(5, "covid_deaths")["county"].tolist()
by_rate  = totals.nlargest(5, "rate_per_100k")["county"].tolist()

print("by count:", by_count)
print("by rate: ", by_rate)
print("shared:  ", set(by_count) & set(by_rate))
print()
print("rate vs population:", round(totals["rate_per_100k"].corr(totals["population_2023"]), 3))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_rates
#| hint: true
# The blank is population_2023.
#
# The two lists have no county in common. Counts correlate with population
# at +0.946 — a chart of counts is close to a chart of where people live.
# Dividing by population takes that out; the rate correlates at -0.232.
# Neither ranking is wrong. They answer different questions, and the error
# is choosing without noticing there was a choice.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_rates
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")

totals = (covid.groupby("county", as_index=False)["covid_deaths"].sum()
               .merge(counties[["county", "population_2023"]], on="county"))

totals["rate_per_100k"] = totals["covid_deaths"] / totals["population_2023"] * 100000

by_count = totals.nlargest(5, "covid_deaths")["county"].tolist()
by_rate  = totals.nlargest(5, "rate_per_100k")["county"].tolist()

print("by count:", by_count)
print("by rate: ", by_rate)
print("shared:  ", set(by_count) & set(by_rate))
print()
print("rate vs population:", round(totals["rate_per_100k"].corr(totals["population_2023"]), 3))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_rates
#| check: true
assert "Philadelphia" in by_count, "Philadelphia leads on total deaths."
assert "Potter" in by_rate, "Potter County leads on deaths per 100,000."
assert len(set(by_count) & set(by_rate)) == 0, "The two lists share no counties."
assert abs(totals["rate_per_100k"].max() - 556.3) < 1.0, "Potter reaches 556 per 100,000."
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The question to ask of every figure of counts
**Does this bar get longer simply because more people live there?** If the answer is yes, the
figure is a population map wearing a health label.
:::

# Exercise 9 — Repair a truncated axis {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 9 — Repair a truncated axis {.smaller}

**This figure runs without error and it is misleading.** A bar encodes value by length, so its
baseline must be zero. `set_ylim(10.2, 10.9)` breaks the correspondence between length and value.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Misleading bar chart of mean adult asthma prevalence for six Pennsylvania regions with the y-axis truncated to the range 10.2 to 10.9 percent, which makes a 0.36 point spread look like a large difference."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "region"]], on="county", how="left")

by_region = joined.groupby("region")["asthma_prev_pct"].mean().sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.bar(by_region.index, by_region.values, color="#003594")
ax.set_ylim(10.2, 10.9)          # <- the distortion
ax.set_ylabel("Mean adult asthma (%)")
ax.set_title("MISLEADING: regional asthma differences look large")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 8.** Misleading bar chart of mean adult asthma prevalence for six Pennsylvania regions with the y-axis truncated to the range 10.2 to 10.9 percent, which makes a 0.36 point spread look like a large difference.
:::

# Exercise 11 — Repair a misleading denominator {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 11 — Repair a misleading denominator {.smaller}

**This figure runs without error and it states something false.** It is titled as a map of
where overdose deaths hit hardest, and it plots raw counts — so it ranks counties by population.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Misleading horizontal bar chart of raw overdose death counts for six Pennsylvania counties in 2023, which ranks the counties by population rather than by mortality burden."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

overdose = pd.read_csv("data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv")
recent = overdose[overdose["year"] == 2023].dropna(subset=["overdose_deaths"])

top = recent.nlargest(6, "overdose_deaths").sort_values("overdose_deaths")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.barh(top["county"], top["overdose_deaths"], color="#003594")
ax.set_xlabel("Overdose deaths")
ax.set_title("MISLEADING: 'where the overdose crisis hit hardest', 2023")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Exercise 12 — The closing figure {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 12 — The closing figure {.smaller}

**Worked example.** Every requirement in this lab, applied at once: labelled axes with units, a
title carrying the finding, a source note, two channels for the grouping, and annotation for
orientation. This is the standard for figures submitted in this course.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Box plot of adult smoking prevalence for metro and nonmetro Pennsylvania counties, with nonmetro counties centred higher at about 18.6 percent against 16.0 percent for metro counties."
import micropip
await micropip.install("seaborn")
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "metro"]], on="county", how="left")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
sns.boxplot(data=joined, x="metro", y="smoking_prev_pct",
            hue="metro", legend=False,
            palette=["#003594", "#8a6400"], ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title("Smoking prevalence by metro status")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 11.** Box plot of adult smoking prevalence for metro and nonmetro Pennsylvania counties, with nonmetro counties centred higher at about 18.6 percent against 16.0 percent for metro counties.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex12_closing
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "metro"]], on="county", how="left")

r = joined["smoking_prev_pct"].corr(joined["asthma_prev_pct"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6))
for group, colour, marker in [("Metro", "#003594", "o"), ("Nonmetro", "#8a6400", "^")]:
    subset = joined[joined["metro"] == group]
    ax.scatter(subset["smoking_prev_pct"], subset["asthma_prev_pct"],
               color=colour, marker=marker, s=44, alpha=0.85,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5, label=group)

for name in ["Chester", "Sullivan"]:
    row = joined[joined["county"] == name].iloc[0]
    ax.annotate(name, (row["smoking_prev_pct"], row["asthma_prev_pct"]),
                xytext=(6, -9), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)

ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title(f"Asthma against smoking, 67 PA counties (r = {r:.3f})")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
ax.text(0.01, 0.98, "Source: CDC PLACES 2024", transform=ax.transAxes,
        fontsize=7, color="#6b7280", verticalalignment="top")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("r =", round(r, 3))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex12_closing
#| check: true
assert abs(r - 0.6593) < 0.01, "Smoking and asthma correlate at +0.659."
assert ax.get_legend() is not None, "Two series require a legend."
assert len(ax.collections) == 2, "One scatter series per metro group."
annotations = [t.get_text() for t in ax.texts]
assert "Chester" in annotations, "Annotate Chester."
assert "Sullivan" in annotations, "Annotate Sullivan — the opposite corner of the figure."

assert ax.get_xlabel() != "" and ax.get_ylabel() != "", "Label both axes."
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What this figure earns, and what it does not
Asthma prevalence and smoking prevalence move together across Pennsylvania counties at
**+0.659**. That is co-movement between **county averages**. It is consistent with smoking
causing asthma, with both sharing upstream causes such as income, occupation, and housing, and
with combinations of the two. **The figure earns the relationship. It does not earn the
mechanism.**
:::

# Done {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## What this lab covered {.smaller}

- `plt.subplots()`, and the **figure/axes** distinction
- `ax.bar()`, `ax.hist()`, `ax.scatter()`, `ax.plot()` — and the question each answers
- **Zero baselines** for bars; the ordered axis a line requires
- Labels with units, titles carrying the finding, source notes, legends
- **Multi-panel grids** indexed `axes[row, col]`
- seaborn via `micropip`, with an **explicit palette** rather than the default
- **Accessibility**: alt text, marks at 3:1, and a second channel for every grouping
- `.corr()` as co-movement between counties, never as cause
- **Rates against counts** — the denominator question

::: {.callout-tip}
## Three of these figures raised no error and were wrong
Exercises 9, 10, and 11 executed cleanly. One truncated an axis, one was unreadable to a
screen reader, and one ranked counties by population while claiming to rank them by burden.
**Running is not checking.**
:::

**Module 6 assembles the whole pipeline — import, clean, join, group, summarise, visualise,
report — into one reproducible document, and it is where the final project begins.**
